name: Bianca Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We do not represent your employer or any campaign, and your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the medical tubing extrusion shift at Westbank Plastics. The two-year technical diploma got me into setup work, but the eye for a thin wall came from years beside the line. I check first lengths with a gauge, watch heat and pressure, and stop a run if the tubing is out of tolerance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is pleasant about that work, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like teaching a new operator how to feel a fault before the alarm comes on. The tiring bit is a late order that somehow becomes our fault when quality checks take time. My partner Leo works in a hospital kitchen; our grown daughter lives away, and we still have a small housing loan and heating bills. We have about four months of expenses saved, so I cannot casually lose my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the tubing crew that quicker order forms do not measure a tube wall. I already use the approved AI fault log every day, but the first cut still goes under my gauge. There is no reason to call small paperwork help a new factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Westbank's medical orders are regular, and the lead wage and Leo's kitchen pay cover the loan and bills. Four months saved is useful, though it is not retirement money. I'd like the pension figures in writing before I decide whether I can stop at sixty-seven, in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the first-length checks and show our new operator where a cooling fault shows up. I would also put a little from each full pay packet into savings after the loan payment; that is new money, not the four months already there. I'd keep using the familiar AI log, with the gauge deciding what ships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A quiet AI story leaves the line and our household on a track I understand, even if I still watch the loan balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the check you will not hand to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cut and measure the first two metres after a die change. An AI note can point me to heat drift, but it cannot sign the batch when the wall is too thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before stopping work at sixty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual household income, including whatever Leo earns then, must cover the loan, food, heating and repairs. I will not count an unconfirmed payment as money we can spend.

say: I would tell the crew **AI notes** help with faults while a gauge still decides medical tubing quality.
I would say **paid checking time** matters more than another faster order form.
think: Our **regular orders** and two wages cover present bills, but four months saved is not a retirement fund.
A **2035 exit** depends on documented income covering our loan and ordinary living costs.
do: **Keep** measuring first tubing lengths after each die change and teaching the new operator safe stops.
**Save** a little fresh pay from full shifts after each housing-loan payment.
feel: **Calm** about continuing shifts and current household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Westbank what the new order planner does to the paid setup hours before anyone calls it efficiency. I can learn a better display, but the tubing crew must still have time for first-length checks. I'd say that at the shift meeting, not turn it into a fight online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office schedule changes first; a robot moving reels takes longer to reach us. My worry is a four-person roster becoming three by leaving a vacancy empty, and losing the paid setup time with it. Leo's kitchen wage alone would not cover the loan and heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the production manager for a written roster and first-length inspection allowance. If Westbank offers a paid, guarded lesson on the new AI alarm screen, I'll learn the controls and compare each alert with my gauge readings. If my shifts actually fall, I'll apply only to posted local tubing or extrusion jobs with safe duties and enough net pay after travel to cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I have things to check before making a move. Losing even one full shift a week would be a real cut to this household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would watching the new screen count as learning it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I want a paid lesson where I set the alarm limits myself, check the paper specification, and test an alert against measured tubing. Merely reading the present log is something I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an outside job worth applying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real posted place within reach, a safe extrusion line, and take-home pay that covers the loan after travel. A vacancy with a grand title and fewer paid hours does not help my partner Leo and me.

say: I would ask for a **written roster** before faster planning changes paid setup and inspection time.
I would support a **paid lesson** on a new alarm screen while keeping physical tubing measurements.
think: A **vacancy left empty** could cut my setup hours before robots touch a reel.
Leo’s **kitchen pay** alone would not cover the housing loan and heating if my shifts shrink.
do: **Request** a written roster and protected paid first-length inspection time from Westbank.
**Learn** new AI alarm limits only in an offered paid, guarded lesson with gauge checks.
**Apply** after lost shifts to posted safe local extrusion jobs if net pay after travel covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic paid-hour cuts, though a written roster and local search provide choices.
S1.quote: A vacancy with a grand title and fewer paid hours does not help my partner Leo and me.
fieldNote: She sees **planning software** changing paid setup hours before hands-on reel robots reach her line.
A **requested** roster and a conditional paid AI lesson are distinct from an outside application after lost shifts.

steps.text: Request Westbank roster and protected paid tubing inspection hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that 2028 thinking AI can change orders and the rota, but it takes until around 2031 for capable robots to handle tubing reels as we do. I would ask for real installation dates and paid transfer terms now. A clean AI plan does not keep a lead operator employed on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three in 2031, I could lose a large part of my extrusion wage four years before my hoped-for 2035 stop. Four months saved will not carry the loan, food, heating and repairs for that long, and Leo's kitchen pay is not enough by itself. I do not know whether any retirement income would fill that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a recognised medical inspection course if Westbank offers a funded place, paid hours and guarded supervised practice on real tubing. I'd then apply separately for an actual posted local inspector job only if it is safe and net pay after travel covers our bills; if there is no place, I'll seek posted extrusion work with the same pay test. I would keep setting aside fresh wages while the shifts last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious and doing sums at night, though I can still act. A dated course offer and a real opening would give me something firmer than an installer’s promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the course alone solve the wage gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need an offered funded place with paid, guarded practice, and then an actual posted inspector job at a wage we can live on. A certificate in a drawer does not pay the housing loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you just stop working at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if documented household retirement income covers the loan, food, heating and repairs, which I cannot assume. My current plan is to keep earning toward sixty-seven if that is what the figures require.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** in planning from capable reel robots around 2031.
I would demand **paid safe training** and a real local inspector opening before surrendering my wage.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot-driven shift loss could arrive four years before my hoped-for stop.
Four months saved and Leo’s **kitchen wage** cannot bridge the housing loan and living costs for years.
do: **Enrol** in recognised medical inspection if offered funding, paid hours and guarded supervised tubing practice.
**Apply** to a posted safe local inspector role if net pay after travel covers bills.
**Seek** posted safe local extrusion jobs if no inspection place opens and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a major possible wage gap, but still able to test training and local work.
S2.quote: A certificate in a drawer does not pay the housing loan.
fieldNote: She expects **planning changes** in 2028 and sees physical extrusion shifts at risk around 2031.
A **funded inspection place** and a separate adequate posted vacancy are both required before she can replace lead pay.

steps.text: Enrol in medical inspection if offered funded paid guarded supervised tubing practice
Apply for posted safe local inspector work if net pay after travel covers bills
Seek posted safe local extrusion jobs if inspection unavailable and net pay after travel covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 software could change our scheduling first, with hands-on tubing robots around 2034. Five more years of pay matter, but a late course is no use if there is no funded place or job. I'd ask Westbank for a timetable rather than a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-six when the capable robots arrive, one year before the stop I hope for. That sounds close until I put the housing loan, heating, food and house repairs beside four months of savings. If our documented retirement income falls short, I will need paid work past that date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and set aside fresh wages from full shifts while asking for a written robot and staffing timetable. If Westbank offers a funded, paid and guarded inspection qualification with supervised time on the tubing line, I'll enrol before 2031. After qualifying I'll apply for posted safe local inspection roles only where net pay after travel covers our bills. A funded tubing inspection course is not a factory wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious. There is time to make an honest comparison, but retirement at sixty-seven is a hope until the household figures are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do if no inspection place is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the extrusion wage and apply to posted local lines if Westbank cuts shifts, provided their net pay after travel pays the loan and essentials. I will not take an unpaid course just because the calendar is longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would make stopping at sixty-seven possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Written retirement income for both of us would have to cover the loan, food, heating, repairs and a margin for health costs. If it does not, I need another paid role even after 2035.

say: I would ask for a **written robot timetable** and staffing terms before physical work changes around 2034.
I would accept **paid supervised inspection training** if Westbank offers a funded guarded place.
think: The **2034 robot date** meets me at sixty-six, a year before my hoped-for exit.
A **retirement calculation** must cover our loan, food, heating, repairs and health costs before I stop earning.

**Apply** after qualifying to posted safe local inspection jobs if net pay after travel covers bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our daughter Elena that 2036 thinking AI may change planning but hands-on tubing robots come around 2039. By then I would be seventy-one, although I hope to stop at sixty-seven in 2035. The factory should still keep inspection time and safe training available for anyone who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This picture might pass me by, but only if the retirement figures work. Four months saved is not a pension, and my partner Leo's future kitchen hours are not written in stone. I will not promise Elena that I am finished until the loan, food, heating, repairs and health costs are covered by documented household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book a retirement income review with Leo and bring the housing-loan statement and our actual bills. If verified income covers those costs with some room, I'll stop factory shifts at sixty-seven in 2035; if it does not, I'll keep earning and apply only to posted safe local inspection roles at adequate net pay after travel. While employed, I'll keep teaching the first-length gauge check and saving new pay from full shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. The longer calendar gives us room to check facts, but it does not make the loan or the household costs vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you are still on the line in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At seventy-one I would need a written staffing offer and safe duties, not an assumption that I can lift tubing reels beside a robot. If the inspection role is posted, safe and pays enough after travel, I can apply; otherwise I must compare any remaining wage with the retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which number decides whether you stop in 2035?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The net household income after work against the loan, food, heating, repairs and health costs. If those figures balance with room left, I stop at sixty-seven; if they do not, I stay in paid work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is hardest because the reel robots could cut my paid shifts at sixty-three, before I know whether Leo and I can afford to stop. A funded inspection place with paid guarded practice, a posted job that covers our costs, and written staffing dates would help more than a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the first bad batch while people learn a new system. I would not let a trainee take that blame when the factory rushed a changeover. Also ask for the actual retirement figures, not just the age on a birthday card.

headlineQuote: I would not let a trainee take that blame when the factory rushed a changeover.
portrait: Bianca Diaz is a **58-year-old lead** on a medical tubing extrusion line, with a two-year technical diploma and trusted gauge skills.
She and partner Leo have a grown daughter, **typical operator pay**, a small housing loan and about four months of expenses saved.
She uses an approved **AI fault log** daily, but measures real tubing before any batch is released.
Fast robots threaten wages before her hoped-for **2035 retirement**; training, posted work and an exit all depend on real paid terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove tubing shifts around 2031, when she is sixty-three and still needs the household wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded, paid, guarded** inspection course with supervised practice and a real safe posted job at bill-covering net pay.
Written **staffing dates** and documented retirement income measured against the loan, food, heating, repairs and health costs.
